tagline: An old freight road crosses mountain grades and railroad country.
intro: The Northwestern Turnpike byway follows US 50 across West Virginia’s Taylor and Preston counties, over Laurel and Cheat mountains. Cheat brings a three-mile, 9 percent grade and 28 curves; Laurel has 8 percent grades on both faces. The state’s Byways and Backways guide records designation in June 1996 and highlights mountain valleys, Cathedral State Park’s virgin forest and Grafton’s railroad heritage. It gives the 54-mile drive an allowance of 1½ hours.

Virginia’s General Assembly chose a turnpike route in 1827 that proved too difficult to build; a new route was commissioned in 1830. The finished road carried freight and settlers west. Turnpike commerce, followed by industry spurred by the parallel Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, helped create the communities along it. US 50 follows the turnpike’s basic alignment. Historian J. M. Callahan’s 1913 account identifies Claudius Crozet as chief engineer and describes an 1831 act allowing toll gates on completed twenty-mile sections. It records the road opening westward to Clarksburg and Parkersburg by 1838.

Traveling east, pass Pruntytown and Grafton, then Thornton and Evansville on the old turnpike corridor. At Erwin, US 50 meets the east bank of the Cheat River near Wolf Creek. Continue toward Aurora and the Maryland line, with Cathedral State Park east of Aurora.

moments.title: Pruntytown
moments.text: Pruntytown’s earlier name, Cross Roads, described its place at the meeting of the Clarksburg Pike and the Beverly and Fairmont Road. An 1835 gazetteer counted 18 houses and 110 people, with a tavern, tanyard, saddlers and two smith shops among the businesses. The town served as Taylor County’s seat from 1844 until an 1878 election moved that role to Grafton. The main post office moved too, and Pruntytown declined. The crossroads remains: US 50 and US 250 meet here. Beulah Baptist Church’s present building dates to 1848, when Pruntytown was still the county seat.

moments.title: Grafton
moments.text: On Main Street, Andrews Methodist Episcopal Church links Grafton to the campaign for Mother’s Day. It held the first official celebration in 1908. Anna Jarvis conceived the holiday to honor mothers’ service to their families and to remember her mother, Ann Maria Reeves Jarvis, who died in 1905. She campaigned for official recognition; President Woodrow Wilson’s 1914 proclamation called for flags on the second Sunday in May. The church became the International Mother’s Day Shrine in 1962. Its stained glass replaced plain windows in 1903, five years before the first Mother’s Day celebration.

moments.title: Cathedral State Park
moments.text: Eastern hemlock predominates in Cathedral State Park’s mixed forest, where Rhine Creek runs through 132 acres. The park contains West Virginia’s largest remaining tract of virgin timber, with trees reaching 90 feet high and 16 feet in circumference. Branson Haas, a Brookside hotel workman, bought the land in 1922 and sold it to the state in 1942. The forest has suffered major losses: lightning felled the state’s largest hemlock in 2004, and Hurricane Sandy’s snowfall caused extensive damage in 2012. The state’s byway guide singles out these virgin stands near Aurora among the route’s special features.
